PROJECT SUMMARY
The opioid crisis is an ongoing urgent national public health emergency in the United States affecting 6.1 million Americans with opioid use disorder (OUD). The increasing prevalence of OUD, favorable reimbursement environment, such as Medicare reimbursement for medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD), and fragmentation of independent providers has garnered interest from financial firms like PE. PE firms acquire a company to enhance its value and resell (exit) within three years, raising concerns that PE’s emphasis on short-term profitability can result in undesirable effects on patient access and outcomes. Based on preliminary data, PE firms have acquired more than 5000 mental health and substance use disorder treatment facilities (SUDTF) that treat OUD in all 50 states as of 2022. Despite this growth, the impact of PE acquisitions on patient care for individuals with OUD is unknown. In this mixed-methods proposal, we aim to generate critical evidence on how PE acquisitions of SUDTF drive differences in patient care for individuals with OUD. We will use a secret shopper approach to evaluate the services offered to individuals with OUD and the patient populations
results.project_title: Private Equity and Opioid Use Disorder

Project Summary/Abstract
Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a growing public health issue in the United States, affecting 5.7 million
individuals in 2023, more than doubling the 2.5 million from 2021. The annual economic burden (~$1.5 trillion)
and opioid-related deaths (54,743 in 2024) underscore the severity of the crisis. While medications for OUD
(MOUD) including buprenorphine are effective, only 25% of those with OUD received MOUD in 2022. OUD care
is complicated by the fact that two-thirds of patients have mental disorders, with over 65% experiencing
depression and/or anxiety. More than half of patients discontinue buprenorphine within 6 months, partly due to
inadequate mental health support. Despite psychiatric treatment’s role in reducing mortality and other adverse
outcomes, access is limited, making primary care settings the largest and fastest-growing providers of MOUD.

PROJECT SUMMARY
Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a public health crisis. First-line pharmacological treatments for OUD
include methadone, which decreases drug use and improves mental and physical health. At treatment onset it
takes weeks to titrate up to a final effective methadone dose, and during this time individuals experience
distressing withdrawal symptoms, especially craving, negative affect, insomnia, and chronic pain. These
symptoms alter decision making and motivate drug use to relieve the aversive state. As such, treatment
cessation rates are high with most dropouts occurring in the first three months; previous research has identified
three months as the minimum amount of time necessary to achieve positive long-term outcomes. This presents
an urgent need to develop adjunctive interventions that reduce OUD symptom severity during the initial weeks
of methadone treatment.

ketamine treatment regimen for individuals initiating methadone therapy at the University of Maryland,

promise to advance knowledge of the molecular neurobiology of disease. However, to date, only a small number
of studies exist, mostly assessing the transcriptome by `RNA-seq', with while chromatin mapping in diseased
human brain has barely begun. This is unsurprising because conventional chromatin accessibility assays and
PCR-amplified libraries with insert sizes of 0.1-0.2 kb face significant shortcomings including (i) lack of resolution
